title: TypeScript null safety versus C# nullable reference types
hook: Both TypeScript strictNullChecks and C# nullable reference types (NRT) catch null mistakes at compile time — neither prevents a malicious JSON payload from delivering null at runtime. Senior interviews love this comparison.

blocks.text: **TypeScript strictNullChecks** splits `null` and `undefined` from other types unless you union them (`string | null`). **C# nullable reference types (NRT)** annotate reference types as nullable (`string?`) or non-nullable (`string`) with compiler warnings. Both are **opt-in on legacy codebases**, default-on in modern templates, and **erased at runtime** — the CLR does not enforce NRT; TypeScript does not emit null checks. Both require **boundary validation** for external data (HTTP, JSON, databases).

blocks.text: Full-stack engineers moving between Angular/Node and ASP.NET need a crisp comparison — Reddit and LeetCode discussions rank this in top TypeScript vs C# questions. Misconception: 'We enabled nullable types so we are null-safe' — production still needs guards at deserialization. Another trap: C# value types use `Nullable<T>` / `T?` for value nullability; TypeScript has no separate value-type layer — everything is union-based.

blocks.title: Compile-time only — both stacks
blocks.body: JsonSerializer.Deserialize<User>(maliciousJson) can still produce null properties in C#. JSON.parse + cast in TS is worse — no runtime types at all.

snippet.label: TypeScript strict null flow
snippet.explanation: Return type documents null. Caller must narrow before property access — parallel to C# if (user is null).

snippet.label: C# NRT equivalent
snippet.explanation: User? marks nullable return. Pattern match narrows — same control flow as TS if (user === null).

snippet.label: Boundary — both stacks need validation
snippet.explanation: strictNullChecks does not parse JSON. Zod provides runtime null/shape checks — like FluentValidation + NRT in C# APIs.

snippet.label: Failure mode — lying to the compiler
snippet.explanation: Type assertion bypasses checking. C# cast (User)json has same lie. Both need real validation.

blocks.title: Assuming parity is identity
blocks.body: TS has both null and undefined; C# NRT focuses on reference null. Model API null vs missing explicitly in TS.

blocks.text: Migration: TS enables strict per package via project references; C# uses nullable context per project. Nullable value types in C# (int?) box; TS number | null is a union with no boxing. C# Maybe<T> libraries vs TS Option types. Interop: generating TS from OpenAPI should mark optional vs nullable fields differently. Senior answer: both are static analysis; invest in boundary schemas; ban ! in code review except framework hooks.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected
blocks.body: Claiming strictNullChecks is runtime safe. Not knowing C# NRT is also compile-time. Unable to explain null vs undefined in TS. No mention of boundary validation.

interviewTakeaways: Both strictNullChecks and C# NRT are compile-time — runtime null still possible.
TS: string | null | undefined unions. C#: string? for references.
Both use ! to suppress warnings without runtime checks.
60s: Same goal — catch null early. Neither validates JSON. TS has null AND undefined. Narrow at boundaries with guards/schemas. ! is last resort.
Follow-up: how would you migrate a legacy codebase to strict null?
commonPitfalls: Weak: NRT/strictNullChecks prevent runtime null — they do not.
Weak: TS ? equals C# ? — different semantics (optional vs nullable).
Strong: Compile-time cousins. Validate boundaries. Union null explicitly. Ban assertion abuse. Know undefined is TS-specific.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS has two nullish values with no compiler — strictNullChecks forces explicit modeling that JS lacks.
Both TS and C# need runtime schemas at API edges — compile-time null safety stops at the process boundary.
